title: Breathing and Healing in Africa, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett shares an experience from visiting Kenya where they spent time with Marcy Okumu, a young woman they were sponsoring through a charity project, which shifted their perspective on reality and highlighted the importance of humility and awareness as they witnessed stark contrasts between wealth and poverty. This experience allowed them to gain a deeper understanding of life in Kenya and the complexities that come with it. Through this encounter, Nomon was reminded of the need for awareness and compassion in our daily lives.

sentences.text: Well, good evening everybody.
This looks a little different from usual.
Last week I told the story of the trip I took to Africa, what it was connected to, and why I went there in July.
That was recorded, so if you missed it and you're interested, you can listen.
This week I thought I'd show the story of the trip.

I had a clearer way of saying this in my mind a minute ago: last week I talked about the heart of it, and now I thought I'd show you the details and the images that were involved in that experience for me.
We'll see how it goes.
It starts with oil money.

The United Arab Emirates, with a huge injection of cash, has created this enormous fleet of Boeing 777 flights, an enormous palace of an airport, and a huge airline staffed by beautiful women in funny hats. [unclear: "I don't have a good pin."] They all have bright red lipstick, which must be expected, matching the hat.
Here's the palace that you arrive at in Dubai after being on the airplane for 15 hours, and they treat you like royalty.
It's very nice.
Then you hang around in Dubai, either overnight or for five hours until three in the morning, and take another flight, and you land in Nairobi, which is where I was going.
So this is the story of my trip to Kenya.

Just briefly on the back story, and you can hear more in the other talk: for the last 10 years, my wife and I have been sponsoring a young woman who was an orphan, an orphan by AIDS, a village girl from Western Kenya.
She's from over here.
We helped her get into school, into boarding high school, into university, and now she's graduating with her master's degree in human development.
All this was done at a distance, like a donation project, a charity project, responding to messages.
So this is her, a real person, a few phone calls, but a little bit at a distance, and now she's no longer at a distance.
This is within the first few minutes of meeting her.
Marcy Okumu is her name.
I was explaining last week one of the ironic things about the first few moments of meeting her: realizing that all these years we weren't even saying her name right.
It's written out M-E-R-C-Y, Mercy, a Christian name, but in Kenyan English the E is pronounced more like "ah."
So she is Marcy, not Mercy.

By the end of the trip, from being a donation recipient of our family, she really felt like a daughter, and it's really strange to have a daughter whose name you've been mispronouncing and whom you've never met.
Janet got her a necklace for graduation, which she really liked.
There's Marcy going to work.
The other woman, Marcy is on this side, the other woman is Carol.
Carol was the in-country project manager for the first charity that we supported Mercy, Marcy, with, called Slum Doctor Program.

Slum Doctor Program was created by my friend Tim Costello, just out of his own good heart and determination and willingness to be in weird territory that he didn't know, and now he's quite an Africa hand, seemingly.
Tim was an AIDS activist.
He went to an international conference in South Africa, met a doctor from Nairobi, and was really surprised by what he learned.
He ended up creating a whole organization to try to help clinics and efforts to help with the AIDS pandemic in Africa, and the statistics about that are unbelievable.
They ended up hiring Carol to be the in-country person, so I was staying at Carol's house in Nairobi.
Here's another girl involved in this program, named Zilpa, and she's receiving this laptop as a gift from another donor.
What happens when you receive a gift, and we do this a little bit but they really do it in Kenya, is you have to take pictures.
This is about receiving the laptop, and there's about 20 more that I left out.
Carol is a middle class Kenyan person, and my sense of reality was gradually shifting.
This is where I started: a perfectly nice but small house.
Running water, but not hot running water except in the shower, which had this special electric heater, like, I don't know if it would be [unclear: "decoded"] in our country.
And two young boys who love to play video games.
Here I'm getting destroyed playing a soccer video game by Edward, the younger brother.
The next day we headed into town.

Step one is the Bota Bota motorcycle taxi.
You can get pretty far for 50 cents.
No, they don't give you a helmet or anything to hold on to, particularly.
Then to the train.

You get on the train.
Quite a tall step.
Later in the station we saw the old train; this is the new train.
Things are older, things are more crowded.
I didn't want to be a total geek with my camera, but during the train ride I was trying to get some pictures to give an impression of how crowded it was, which I didn't really succeed at.
All the seats filled within the first couple of stops, seats along each side, and then the center started to fill with people standing.
Then people came in and went in between two people who were sitting side by side on the little bucket seats.

And they did, or kind of crammed in.

And now it's totally normal.

People are very well dressed in Kenya.
Everything else is run down.

My host, the husband of Carol, this fellow named Willis, finagled to get us up on the roof of one of the tallest buildings in Kenya.
I don't know if he knew people or if it was a bribe.
We were going through all these security checkpoints.
I really had to learn, through this whole trip, just to tag along.
I didn't know what was going on most of the time.
A lot of things were negotiated and planned in Swahili anyway.
One minute we were at this desk, I don't know what we were doing, and he's saying, "Could you give this lady 300 shillings?"
"Okay, give her 300 shillings."
The next thing I knew, I was on this roof.
We had to go through this construction zone.
There was no fence.
Anyway, lovely guy.
He used to be a safari guide; we'll get to the safari guides.
Now he's a political operative, and politics are very strange and, as he says, very corrupt in Kenya.
One of the jokes of the whole trip, which turned out to be a useful foil, was that I told Marcy and everyone I met that I'm into birds.
I thought that was the funniest thing.
Like, "Why would you be into birds?
Who cares about birds?"
So I stopped and took pictures of birds.
These are Egyptian geese.
We'll do a few more birds.
I mostly weeded out the bird shots, but maybe we'll do another one with bird shots.
There are more species of birds within the city limits of Nairobi than in all of North America: about 500 species right there, and about 1,000 in the country.
It's right by the equator, so higher diversity.
The goal for being in Nairobi was to get a sense of Marcy's life as an educated Kenyan woman.
She has a job in the city.
She has an apartment.
She has friends.
I want to know, what's that like?
What you can see a little bit from these pictures is that there's trash everywhere.
One of the things I learned is that it's our first world privilege to have a low trash environment, and we get so bent out of shape when one little bit of trash is on the ground, right?
Trash all over the place.
Now we're at work.
This is the only place she really has access to a computer with internet access.
I learned this when we were emailing back and forth: she would always be emailing from work.
Nobody can afford internet access at home.
Her work is for an Italian-run NGO, which created a small hospital in an area of Nairobi that has basically no medical services.
I ran into little projects like this everywhere.
Every so often there would be a clinic or a building or a school, and they'd always have a plaque on the front.

That's the plaque right behind us, our heads there, explaining which country and which organization, Rotary, UN, had brought these services here, because the government is not able to provide many services, or chooses not to, depending on one's attitude.
His name was Jacopo.

One of the funny things that Mercy told me later was that they do all their professional writing in English, which is not a first language for either of them, and they go into lots of arguments about what's proper English grammar.
For Mercy, it's a third language.
Her first language is her tribal language of Luo.
Her second language is Swahili, which is a language for communicating with people across the country and across Eastern Africa.
Her third language is English, and it's Jacopo's second language.
So from now on they're going to send reports to my wife, who's quite a good editor.
At least they said they will.
We'll see.
Typical street scene.
All the minor roads are dirt.
Here's a furniture builder.
We're on an outskirts community called Khyambu, and they were outside the gate of Mercy's apartment.
My understanding is gradually adjusting from Carol and Willis and their son's middle class house to the dirt streets and the ditches and trash, and to Mercy's apartment here.
It's a small but perfectly nice apartment, but it's interesting when she showed me the bathroom, which had a toilet and running water, her friends, and everywhere we went I would serve meals.
I ate a lot.
Somehow I lost a little bit of weight, so I don't know how that happened.
I mean, I didn't eat in between these big meals.
Anyway, in the bathroom, just not really taking it in.
That's kind of an amazing thing.
Let's see, where's the video?
Ah, this is the video.
Okay.
Now you can see and hear Mercy giving us a tour of her apartment.
We didn't take it in, what a privilege it is for her to have a room of her own, and a kitchen, and a bathroom.
And these roofs are little houses.
There were zero washing machines, so clothes are all washed by hand, and you'll still see more examples of that later.
We went to the one significant museum in Nairobi, the National Museum.
A perfectly nice place; not so many places like that.
Street scene.
And now here we are getting organized for Kenya's largest tourist industry, which is the industry of having African animals and a big game reserve and taking tourists on safari.
And so with Mercy, and none of her friends had ever been on safari.
Sometimes as a school trip they go on a school bus, to the edge of one of the game parks.
But the safari that all the outside visitors go on, none of the locals go to, partly because it's just too expensive.
Through Willis's connections we managed to finagle a deal.
I had already finagled a bit of a deal, for, I forget, it was like $1,200 for the two of us for three days.
So we got it down to $500, but you can easily spend like $1,000 a person a day on these safaris, for various reasons which we'll get into.
Long, long, long drive across town and up the Rift Valley.
So here's Nairobi, we drive down.
This is a huge valley created by tectonic plate movement, a very fertile valley, and also more or less the birthplace of our species, as best we know.
So that was interesting too, to be in a place and to remind myself from time to time: people have lived here from the beginning, for a million years.
So we're driving across the valley, and then there's a large game reserve here, and then it goes across the border into Tanzania.
Here it's called Masai Mara; there it's called Serengeti, which you've probably heard of.
So it was fascinating.
We haven't quite gotten there, and this was our first big sighting.
We're just cruising along the road after getting through the towns, which are getting smaller and smaller and smaller, and the roads bumpier and bumpier and bumpier.
The last two hours or so we're on dirt roads.
And there's giraffe and some gazelle and maybe a muskox in the back, I'm not sure.
So we're in this van, bumping along.
Part of why ours was affordable is that we're staying in a pretty simple hotel here.
There's our hotel.
Suits me, it's warm everywhere.
And then the next day, these might not always be in the best order, but the next day we cross the nearby gate and go into the park, and it was so stark.
It was going from scattered houses and sheep and goats and all the grass grazed to the ground, to lush grass and African animals just everywhere, just driving along.
I didn't see a fence.
Maybe there was a fence.
It's a huge, huge place.

And so it ended up being beautiful, wonderful.
These are muskox, and no, no, wildebeest, excuse me, wildebeest.

So that's maybe, I don't know, 50 yards away, just walking along.

So it's an industry.

It's not safe.

Africa primeval over here.
Now we're going to her village.
There's a town here called Homa Bay, a little too small for this map, and this is a little lobe of Lake Victoria.

Marcy's used to taking a bus, which takes six to ten hours, in that range, depending what's going on.

He's a piece of cardboard.

I mean, he's a physically large man, a lovely man.
Here he is with his wife, who's called Mama.
I couldn't quite figure out what to call him.
Some people called him Baba, which means father, some people called him Engineer, Engineer, some people called him Honorable.
So I just said hi, I think I said Honorable a few times, sir.
But anyway, let me skip ahead.
Yeah, so here's his house, and again I'm still calibrating.
There's houses like this in Bellingham, and I suppose that's such an unusual house.
But what I gradually realized was this is an enormous house.
This is a palace.
This is Shaki Muni's palace.
He was a successful government engineer.

I don't know what kind of salary government engineers get or how things were when he was working, but the interesting thing is that he chose to move back to the village where he came from and to erect this house.
It's a compound with a staff, and he also does good works.
He is one of the people who helped found the boarding school to which we sent Marcy, and he continues to give donations and help a little bit there.
It was just interesting to be invited into that part of this society, the top of the society in that socioeconomic way.
Lovely people, very friendly.
I was tasked to bring many gifts from Bellingham, so here we're taking pictures because I'm giving gifts.
So he, whoops, no, I wasn't holding it.
Okay, you've got to look right.

Yeah, so he does a lot.
So here we are driving around in his car.

Here's Mercy at the place.

She was a little uncomfortable there because this is her first time being in this house as a guest, being treated as an equal, seated at his table instead of being seated at the servants table and being expected to make conversation.

The amazing thing was that we went to visit Ombogo Girls Academy on a Saturday, and it's a Seventh-day Adventist school.
Almost all the schools are Christian, Seventh-day or Catholic mostly.
So it was time for Saturday service.
As we entered, the girls were singing.

I don't think we have an image of me speaking, but the thing I learned, and I had many such visits to different institutions, schools, orphanages, clinics and stuff like that, is that the guests don't just sit there.

Our sponsor, please speak."

Then there's this whole back and forth about God is great.
There was a time when the guests were each expected to get up and do a call and response.
I thought, "Oh my gosh, what should I do?
It doesn't seem authentic for me to speak about God."
So it occurred to me to create a call and response for them, where I said, "I'll say 'please take care of yourself,' and you'll say 'we will.'" I thought it very simple, and I did that.
I said, "Please, please take care of each other," and they all, in perfect harmony, said, "We will."
So beautiful.
